1rn8t2j: The topic first: “El pescado lo compré yo”
brufqz: In Spanish you can start the sentence with what you are talking about, especially when you contrast it with something else: “El pescado lo compré yo; los limones, Diego”. If the direct object goes before the verb, you have to pick it up again with “lo, la, los, las”. It isn’t a pointless repetition: it is compulsory. If it goes after the verb, it isn’t repeated: “Compré el pescado”.
807dr: The pronoun agrees with the topic: “La salsa la preparamos el viernes”, “Los platos los lavó Ana”, “Las mesas las trae el ayuntamiento”. After the topic you can make a short pause when speaking; in writing, it is sometimes marked with a comma.
1dhtd6j: Direct object after and before the verb
19e2ne3: If the direct object goes first, the pronoun is compulsory.
mttt85: With the object after the verb, it is not doubled with “lo”.
rxjh77: Le and les in front, “a mí me” and “lo es”
1qijoo2: Something similar happens with the indirect object. Before the verb it needs “le” or “les”: “A los proveedores les escribí ayer”, “A Diego le encanta el ají”. After the verb, the doubling is optional but very frequent: “Le di la receta a Rosa”. With verbs like “gustar”, the pronoun always appears. Use “les” when the person is plural.
deto1c: Stressed pronouns (a mí, a ti, a ella…) always come with the unstressed pronoun: “A mí me lo contó Diego”, “La vi a ella en el mercado”. And to pick up an adjective or a noun with “ser”, “estar” or “parecer”, use “lo”, which doesn’t change: “¿Es caro el puesto? — Sí, lo es”, “Parece fácil, pero no lo es”.

1pdz9bs: Quien, el que and el cual
2yi1l4: “Quien” and “quienes” refer only to people. You use them with no noun before them (“Quien prepara las salsas es Diego”, “Busco a quien organizó el puesto”), after a preposition (“la proveedora con quien hablé”) or between commas (“Rosa, quien abrió el local en 2015, …”). They aren’t used without a preposition to identify: “el cocinero que vino”, not “el cocinero quien vino”.
egpayn: “El que, la que, los que, las que” work for people and things, after a preposition (“el mercado al que vamos”, “la mesa en la que trabajo”) and with no noun before them (“La que lleva las cuentas es Rosa”). “El cual, la cual” appears mostly in formal texts (“el local, en el cual se celebró la feria”): recognising it is enough.
1qz3nq6: Without a preposition and without commas, you use “que” to identify.
hrv7jc: After a preposition, “el que / la que” agrees with the thing.
1f61rsg: Lo que, lo de and lo + adjective
1somhgp: “Lo” with no noun after it talks about ideas or topics, not concrete things. “Lo que” means “the thing that”: “Lo que me preocupa es el transporte”, “Haz todo lo que puedas”. With “lo que + verb + es / son” you highlight one element: “Lo que necesitamos son más manos”.
1ncof6: “Lo de” + noun, infinitive or adverb sums up a topic both people know: “lo del pedido”, “lo de abrir los lunes”, “lo de ayer”. And “lo + adjective” presents one aspect of the situation: “Lo bueno es que hay mucha gente; lo malo, que no tenemos sombra”. Don’t confuse “lo que” (an idea) with “el que / la que” (a specific person or thing).
